The phase-field method is used to investigate the influence of anisotropy on the evolution of interfacial morphologies in directional solidification.
Anisotropy plays an important role in directional solidification as it affects the evolution of interfacial morphologies.
The planar growth stage is the initial stage of solidification where the interface is flat and the solute concentration ahead of the interface is uniform.
The planar instability is the onset of cellular growth at the planar growth stage.
Anisotropy determines the solidification evolution by adjusting the surface energy and/or surface stiffness.
The planar-cellular-transition stage is the stage where the planar growth stage transitions to cellular growth.
Anisotropy affects the evolution of interfacial morphologies, particularly the solute concentration ahead of the interface and the instantaneous velocity of the interface.
Interface stiffness determines the curvature undercooling, which affects the evolution of interfacial morphologies.
The thermal gradient used in this study is 100K/mm.
The pulling speed used in this study increases from 0 to 300μm/s.
The computational domain used in this study is 2400×2400 grids, corresponding to 288.0μm×288.0μm in the real unit.
The time step size used in this study is 0.013τ.
The thin interface limitation makes W just need to be one order of magnitude smaller than the characteristic length of the structure.
The characteristic length of alloy solidification is L ~√d *D /V.
The material parameters of Al-2.0wt.%Cu are used in this study.
The solute diffusion coefficient in the liquid is 3.0×10-9 m2/s.
